title: Microsoft Dynamics Alternatives: 7 CRM Solutions That Cut Costs and Fit Your Workflow (2026)
summary: Compare the best Microsoft Dynamics alternatives for 2026. Save on CRM costs with these top solutions for customization, flexibility, and value.
body_text: TL;DR: The best Microsoft Dynamics alternatives in 2026 are Salesforce Sales Cloud for deep customization, HubSpot CRM for simplicity, Zoho CRM for affordability, Freshsales for sales automation, SAP Sales Cloud for enterprise needs, Pipedrive for deal management, and Miniloop for companies seeking a custom-built CRM that cuts costs by 5x to significantly and shifts from per-seat licenses to true workflow fit. Microsoft Dynamics Alternatives: 7 CRM Solutions That Cut Costs and Fit Your Workflow (2026) Last updated: August 2026 The top microsoft dynamics alternatives are Miniloop (best for custom workflows and cost savings), Salesforce Sales Cloud (deepest customization and feature breadth), HubSpot CRM (most user-friendly (free tier)), Zoho CRM (best value for SMBs), Freshsales (best for sales automation). In 2026, more teams are re-evaluating their CRM investments as licensing models, platform complexity, and cost-overruns with Microsoft Dynamics 365 grow impossible to ignore. CRM buyers are asking not only 'what will fit our team today?', but also 'how do we avoid hidden per-seat fees and run our own workflows. And not the vendor's defaults?’ New options now make it possible to prioritize cost savings, flexibility, and infrastructure independence over one-size-fits-all feature lists. Why people look for Microsoft Dynamics alternatives Microsoft Dynamics 365 is recognized for its broad feature set and strong enterprise integrations. However, many businesses find it expensive, complex to implement, and difficult to adapt to their specific workflow needs. High per-seat licensing costs and vendor-driven workflows can turn a powerful solution into an unwieldy, costly investment that no longer fits how teams actually work. This motivates teams to seek alternatives that lower cost, add flexibility, and provide a CRM that is tailored to their real business processes. Microsoft Dynamics vs alternatives: Feature and cost comparison table Microsoft Dynamics 365 uses a subscription model with per-seat pricing and extensive feature modules, making costs unpredictable for businesses with growing teams or custom needs. Compared to its top alternatives, Dynamics offers deep enterprise integration and configurability, but many find the complexity and pricing structure lead them to consider simpler CRMs, custom solutions, or platforms that better match specific use cases. The table below directly contrasts pricing models, customization scope, use-case fit, integration ease, and key limitations for Dynamics and the leading alternatives. CRM Cost Structure Customization Level Best-Fit Use Cases Integration & Migration Ease Notable Limitations Microsoft Dynamics 365 Subscription, per-seat High (modules, configs) Large enterprises, existing MS tech stack Native for Microsoft, moderate complexity for others Overwhelming setup, can be costly Salesforce Sales Cloud Subscription, per-seat High (extensible) Enterprise sales, deep integrations Strong ecosystem, complex migration High learning curve, premium cost HubSpot CRM Freemium & paid, per-seat Basic-to-moderate SMBs, fast onboarding, marketing focus Smooth for popular tools, simple Advanced features gated, limited automation Zoho CRM Tiered, per-seat Moderate Cost-conscious teams, broad functionality Broad integration support Some module complexity, can require tweaks Pipedrive Tiered, per-seat Moderate Sales pipeline-centric teams Quick setup, easy migration Limited marketing/automation depth Freshsales Tiered, per-seat Moderate-to-high Sales automation, customer engagement Integrates with Freshworks suite Fewer enterprise features, not for all industries SAP Sales Cloud Custom enterprise pricing High (SAP ecosystem) Global enterprises, existing SAP users Native SAP, complex external Very high complexity, slow deployment Insightly Tiered, per-seat Moderate Teams needing CRM + project management Integrates with G Suite, MS 365 Less enterprise depth, project focus may distract This at-a-glance table highlights the trade-offs faced by teams evaluating CRM options: Dynamics and Salesforce lead on enterprise features and ecosystem depth but require significant investment in both budget and onboarding. HubSpot and Pipedrive appeal to organizations prioritizing speed and simplicity, while Zoho offers a middle ground of breadth and affordability. SAP and Insightly target specific stack or project needs respectively. But each alternative brings inherent limitations tied to its pricing model and customization ceiling. For teams seeking workflow-matched customization and full infrastructure flexibility without per-user costs, these mainstream options often leave notable gaps. For maximum workflow fit and cost reduction: Miniloop Miniloop is built for companies that have outgrown the constraints of generic, off-the-shelf CRMs and need a system engineered around their unique workflows. Unlike traditional platforms that force your processes to fit their pre-made modules, Miniloop delivers custom CRM development. Aligning the full system to your specific business logic and operations. This approach means no more stringing together workarounds for core functions or wrestling with features you don’t want. Transitioning from an existing CRM? Miniloop handles complete data migration from legacy systems, ensuring business continuity and preserving your operational knowledge. The solution is also designed for infrastructure flexibility: host your CRM on Miniloop’s managed servers or on your own, giving your team control over data residency and compliance. Cost discipline is a core advantage. Miniloop does away with per-seat fees entirely; clients pay for the custom build, ongoing support, and updates, not for every user they add. This setup can cut CRM spending by a factor of five to ten compared to enterprise licenses that accumulate charges as teams scale, especially when headcount is high or workflows are complex. With tailored development, full migration, and infrastructure independence, Miniloop is a match for teams with sizable CRM spending, typically $50,000 or more per year, and requirements that can’t be addressed by mainstream CRMs. It isn’t aimed at startups or small companies on entry-level plans; its strength is in reshaping the economics and effectiveness of CRM for larger organizations with exacting demands. Ditch your expensive CRM subscription Get a custom CRM designed for your workflow at a fraction of the price. Talk to our team to get a fixed quote. Book a call For deep features and enterprise integration: Salesforce Sales Cloud Salesforce Sales Cloud stands out as the go-to CRM for enterprises requiring deep customization, a robust integration ecosystem, and enterprise-grade features. Its platform is frequently the preferred option for large organizations that need to connect CRM data to hundreds of business tools and manage complex sales or marketing operations at scale. But with these capabilities comes a significant increase in both ongoing cost and administrative complexity when compared to leaner alternatives. Salesforce's strength lies in its ability to mold around highly specialized processes. The Salesforce AppExchange offers one of the broadest third-party integration libraries in the CRM market, enabling businesses to unify workflows across finance, support, analytics, and almost any department. A dedicated suite of development tools allows custom modules, automations, and reporting, giving companies full control over their data structure and workflows. However, such flexibility comes with trade-offs. Unlike tools that emphasize simple onboarding or out-of-the-box usability, Salesforce is known for requiring dedicated admins or consulting partners to ensure initial setup and ongoing health. Licensing fees and user-based pricing quickly climb for growing teams, and customizing features to match unique internal processes can demand additional investment. Many businesses find that embracing the platform's full power requires long-term planning, periodic training, and a willingness to manage evolving system complexity. For organizations with ambitious integration needs and the resources to support a comprehensive CRM environment, Salesforce offers unmatched extensibility and capability. But for teams prioritizing simplicity, lower total cost of ownership, or rapid deployment, alternative solutions may prove a better fit for their workflow and budget. For simplicity and fast onboarding: HubSpot CRM HubSpot CRM is one of the most accessible CRM options available, offering a zero-cost entry point and a simple, intuitive interface that works for small to midsize teams. Its free tier and ease of setup let businesses get started with customer management, pipeline tracking, and basic automation without deep technical overhead, making onboarding as fast as possible for non-specialists. HubSpot’s visual dashboard, integrated contact management, and basic automations are built for clarity. Users with minimal CRM experience can begin tracking leads and closing deals in minutes. This streamlined approach appeals to businesses that need to move quickly and value a clean, guided UX over extensive customization. The platform scales with paid plans as teams grow, offering advanced features for a fee; however, these additions can lead to a much higher monthly cost as organizations need more sophisticated automation, reporting, or integration capabilities. Compared to platforms like Microsoft Dynamics or Salesforce, HubSpot CRM is less suited for businesses that require deeply tailored workflows, heavy process automation, or significant infrastructure control. Customization is limited to what the platform provides, and there’s less flexibility for unique business models or complex integrations. Still, for resource-constrained teams prioritizing rapid deployment and low up-front costs, it's an industry-standard starting point, particularly when overall simplicity and user adoption are top priorities. For affordable, broad functionality: Zoho CRM Zoho CRM stands out as a cost-effective solution for small to midsize businesses seeking a rich feature set without the complexity or price tag of Microsoft Dynamics. Its affordable plans, combined with a wide range of practical tools, make Zoho CRM popular with globally distributed and multi-role teams who need a versatile, accessible CRM platform. While it supports customization and workflow automation, Zoho’s flexibility is best suited to companies with straightforward needs, since deeper configuration is less extensive than what’s possible with Salesforce or Miniloop. Businesses can select from several pricing tiers that scale with usage, minimizing risk for growing teams. The platform includes robust built-in tools such as lead and deal management, sales forecasting, email integration, and automation rules. Even on lower tiers. This mix enables most teams to centralize contacts and activities, run collaborative sales pipelines, and roll out basic automation without costly add-ons or long onboarding cycles. Zoho’s strengths lie in delivering strong value for teams needing essential CRM without enterprise overhead. However, enterprises or businesses requiring heavily tailored workflows and total infrastructure control may find Zoho’s customization limits restrictive. For price-sensitive teams with standard sales or service operations, Zoho CRM delivers an impressive balance of features and simplicity. Advanced requirements or niche processes may prompt consideration of tools purpose-built for customization. For sales teams focused on pipeline management: Pipedrive Pipedrive streamlines pipeline management with a clear, visual interface built specifically for sales teams. Its intuitive drag-and-drop boards make it easy to track leads and deals at every stage. Ideal for organizations wanting a straightforward, affordable tool that keeps the focus on pipeline momentum rather than complex feature sets or admin overhead. Pipedrive is widely recognized as a go-to CRM for small and mid-sized sales-driven teams. Best for: Sales teams prioritizing visual pipeline management and simplicity Key features: Visual sales pipeline board with drag-and-drop deal stages Customizable activity and deal tracking Built-in email integration and tracking Mobile app for on-the-go updates Smart contact data enrichment Deal and activity reporting dashboards Pricing: Essential: $15/user/month (core pipeline and contact management) Advanced: $29/user/month (automation, group emailing) Professional: $59/user/month (more advanced reporting and permissions) Strengths: Pipedrive’s clean visual approach minimizes setup time and makes onboarding simple. Even teams without a dedicated admin can get started quickly. Its pricing and features are accessible to SMBs that find Microsoft Dynamics or Salesforce unnecessarily heavy. Limited admin complexity reduces training needs and ensures data stays current. Weaknesses: Teams seeking deep customization, integrations with legacy systems, or complex automation may find Pipedrive limiting. Its functionality is focused on sales pipelines; broader operational workflows or complex, cross-departmental processes often require workarounds or additional tools. Choose Pipedrive when: You need your team closing deals fast, value ease of use, and can work within Pipedrive’s ready-made sales-focused structure. If your workflow is highly unique or spans multiple departments, or if data ownership and infrastructure flexibility are mission-critical, consider more customizable CRM solutions. For teams focused on sales velocity and simplicity. Pipedrive’s visual pipeline is hard to beat. For advanced automation and customer engagement: Freshsales Freshsales stands out with its strong sales automation and customer engagement tools, making it an excellent fit for scaling sales teams that want robust workflows and communication features without the need for overwhelming enterprise-level integrations. Freshsales' pricing remains competitive for the breadth of its automation offerings, positioning it as a practical option for organizations moving beyond entry-level CRMs and seeking more structure across their sales processes. Best for: Sales teams ready to scale with advanced automation and buyer communication, but not yet in need of enterprise platform complexity. Key features: Visual sales pipeline management for tracking deals in progress Built-in email, phone, and chat for direct customer engagement without switching platforms Automated lead assignment and scoring to focus reps' efforts Activity capture and task reminders to keep teams aligned and persistent Native integrations with popular business tools (like email, calendars, and productivity apps) Reporting dashboards for visibility into sales metrics and pipeline health Pricing: Growth: $15/user/month (core automation and engagement tools) Pro: $39/user/month (expanded automation, AI insights, more customization) Enterprise: $69/user/month (advanced controls, custom modules, deeper analytics) Strengths: Freshsales offers automation capabilities that help teams save time on repetitive tasks and prioritize the right opportunities. The built-in communication suite makes managing outreach and follow-up smooth, all from within the CRM. Weaknesses: Some organizations may find its customization options and integration ecosystem less expansive than bigger platforms like Salesforce or Microsoft Dynamics. Businesses with complex processes or heavy requirements for third-party integrations may eventually grow out of Freshsales. Choose Freshsales when: You want a CRM that brings structure to growing sales teams with a straightforward interface, practical automation, and all-in-one communication channels. Without incurring the higher costs or complexity of full enterprise solutions. For global scale and SAP stack alignment: SAP Sales Cloud SAP Sales Cloud is purpose-built for large, multinational organizations that rely on deep integration with SAP’s full stack. ERP, finance, analytics, and more. Enterprises entrenched in the SAP ecosystem adopt SAP Sales Cloud to achieve smooth data flow across functions and geographies, using unified processes and robust compliance frameworks. However, its powerful infrastructure demands significant investment in setup, configuration, and ongoing management, making it impractical for most SMBs focused on reducing CRM costs and complexity. Best for: Global enterprises invested in the SAP platform Key features: Native integration with SAP ERP and finance systems Multinational sales management and reporting Territory and quota management at global scale Advanced analytics and forecasting tools Role-based access and compliance controls Support for custom business processes via SAP integration Pricing: Custom enterprise pricing. Request a quote Strengths: SAP Sales Cloud tightly unifies with other SAP products, supporting end-to-end workflows across sales, operations, and finance on a single platform. Its architecture accommodates complex needs. Multiple regions, currencies, compliance regimes, and layered approval chains. Weaknesses: The high cost of implementation, ongoing administration, and required SAP expertise puts it out of reach for smaller businesses or those without existing SAP investments. Fast-growing SMBs seeking flexibility and lower overhead typically find the system overly complex for their actual needs. Choose SAP Sales Cloud when: You’re a large enterprise already running SAP and require deep process integration, advanced security, and multinational support. Plus the resources to manage a specialized CRM at scale. If you’re a growth-stage business prioritizing cost savings and agility, SAP Sales Cloud’s complexity and expense make it a poor fit. Automate more than CRM: Where Miniloop fits for growing teams Busy teams outgrow off-the-shelf CRMs because prebuilt solutions often leave them with ongoing manual work: data imports rarely transfer everything cleanly, custom process alignment means clunky workarounds, and every change, whether updating workflows or scaling to new teams, becomes a recurring setup project. These gaps force businesses to revisit the same tasks with each evolution, draining resources and reducing efficiency. Miniloop solves this by delivering fully custom CRM development with built-in support for everything mainstream platforms make manual. Need to migrate full customer histories from a legacy CRM? Miniloop handles migration as a managed process. Instead of shoehorning unique sales or service workflows into a generic mold, Miniloop builds the system around the organization's real operational logic, not the other way around. Regular updates and customizations are part of the ongoing support, removing the cycle of rework as business needs shift. For companies prioritizing data autonomy or compliance, Miniloop's infrastructure flexibility stands apart: deploy on managed servers or run independently on your own systems. There's also operational clarity. Miniloop eliminates per-user licensing and surprise fees, so adding more users or business units won’t balloon costs. This approach means growing businesses can automate more of their CRM workload and control their total spend as they scale. Which Microsoft Dynamics alternative should you choose? The right Microsoft Dynamics alternative comes down to your team’s size, workflow needs, and budget. If your business spends around $50,000 or more annually on CRM and needs processes the standard platforms can’t match, investing in a custom CRM like Miniloop delivers long-term savings through tailored fit and elimination of per-seat fees. For smaller teams, straightforward sales cycles, or lean budgets, off-the-shelf CRMs like HubSpot, Zoho, and Pipedrive provide a more predictable ramp-up with less maintenance overhead. Use the guide below to quickly narrow your options: Team Size Workflow Complexity Annual CRM Budget Best Fit 1–10 Simple <$5,000 HubSpot CRM, Zoho CRM 10–50 Moderate $5,000–$50,000 Pipedrive, Freshsales 50+ Complex, customized $50,000+ Miniloop, Salesforce, SAP A custom CRM is worth it when your processes can’t be mapped cleanly to mainstream software, or when per-seat subscriptions balloon costs far beyond value delivered. Off-the-shelf solutions reduce rollout complexity for standard pipelines but can force you into uncomfortable workarounds as your business scales. Consider your integration requirements, data ownership preferences, and the predictability of your licensing model. For teams planning long-term growth or demanding exact workflow alignment, a custom solution built for your operations provides the control and future-proofing generic platforms can’t. In contrast, businesses prioritizing fast onboarding and extensive prebuilt integrations may prefer sticking with proven mainstream CRMs. Related Reading Orbitly Review 2026: Lead Enrichment, Pricing, and When It Falls Short Hunter.io Review 2026: Features, Pricing, and the Best Alternatives CIENCE Pricing 2026: What You'll Actually Pay for Data + SDRs Zendesk Pricing 2026: What You Need to Know Related Resources Try Miniloop - Start automating your GTM busywork with Miniloop Get in touch - Start a low-pressure conversation with the Miniloop team Templates - Ready-to-run workflow templates Integrations - Connect Miniloop to the tools you already use Frequently Asked Questions What are the main drawbacks of using Microsoft Dynamics 365? Microsoft Dynamics 365 is known for its extensive feature set, but this breadth often comes with significant complexity and a steep learning curve. Many businesses struggle with the high cost associated with per-seat licensing, which can scale quickly as teams grow. Customizing Dynamics to fit unique workflows can be both time-consuming and expensive, frequently requiring external consultants. Additionally, teams sometimes find themselves adapting their processes to the software, rather than the other way around. How do per-seat licensing fees compare across CRM alternatives? Per-seat licensing fees can vary dramatically from vendor to vendor. Platforms like Microsoft Dynamics 365 and Salesforce typically charge significant monthly fees for each user, which can make total costs unpredictable as team sizes fluctuate. Options like HubSpot and Zoho CRM offer lower entry points or even free tiers, but core features may be restricted or accrue extra costs as usage increases. Miniloop stands out by eliminating per-seat fees entirely, charging instead based on the custom features and hosting requirements of each client. How difficult is it to migrate data from Microsoft Dynamics 365 to a new CRM? Migrating data from Microsoft Dynamics 365 can be challenging, especially due to the complexity and amount of custom data fields and relationships it may contain. Most CRM alternatives offer some migration tools, but these may require careful data mapping and manual intervention to ensure a smooth transition. Custom CRMs like Miniloop typically provide comprehensive migration support, handling complex data structures and ensuring business continuity during the switch. Regardless of the chosen alternative, planning and testing are critical for successful data migration. Which alternatives are best for teams requiring deep workflow customization? Salesforce Sales Cloud is widely recognized for its extensive customization capabilities, although customizing it often requires technical resources or outside consulting. Miniloop is specifically designed for organizations that need a fully custom CRM built around their exact workflow, offering tailored development from the ground up. Off-the-shelf CRMs like HubSpot and Zoho provide workflow automations, but may not flexibly accommodate unique processes beyond typical sales or marketing pipelines. Organizations with highly specialized requirements may benefit most from a custom-built solution. Are there CRM options better suited for small businesses than Microsoft Dynamics? Yes, several CRM platforms cater specifically to small businesses with lower pricing, simpler interfaces, and more accessible setup processes than Microsoft Dynamics 365. HubSpot CRM offers a popular free tier and intuitive user experience, making it attractive to small teams. Zoho CRM provides affordable plans with a range of essential features tailored for SMBs. Microsoft Dynamics is generally more suited to larger organizations with complex needs and higher budgets. How do ongoing support and update costs differ between custom and off-the-shelf CRMs? Off-the-shelf CRMs often bundle support and updates into recurring subscription fees, but premium support or advanced customizations can incur extra charges. Businesses using custom-built CRMs typically have more control over support arrangements and may benefit from dedicated assistance tailored to their system. With Miniloop, ongoing support is provided by a team familiar with each client's specific setup, reducing time spent on troubleshooting. The trade-off is that custom solutions may require longer-term commitments for maintenance and periodic feature updates. What is the typical cost-saving potential of moving away from Microsoft Dynamics 365? Switching from Microsoft Dynamics 365 can result in significant cost savings, particularly for organizations with large teams or complex feature needs that drive up licensing expenses. Miniloop, for instance, positions itself as enabling businesses to reduce their CRM costs by five to ten times by eliminating per-seat fees and charging only for necessary features. The actual savings depend on factors like the number of users, required customizations, and hosting preferences. Careful cost modeling is recommended to understand the full savings potential based on an organization’s unique needs. Is it possible to host my CRM on my own infrastructure with any of these alternatives? Most mainstream CRMs, such as Salesforce, HubSpot, and Zoho, are offered exclusively as cloud-based services without the option for on-premises hosting. Solutions like Miniloop provide flexibility by allowing clients to run their CRM on managed servers or their own infrastructure, appealing to organizations that prioritize data ownership and compliance. Having control over infrastructure can be essential for sectors with strict regulatory requirements. It's important to verify hosting options during the CRM selection process if infrastructure independence is a priority. Which CRM supports the fastest onboarding for new users? HubSpot CRM is commonly praised for its intuitive design and straightforward onboarding process, making it easy for new users to become productive quickly. Zoho CRM and Pipedrive also focus on simplicity and offer guided onboarding tools to speed up adoption. On the other end, platforms like Microsoft Dynamics 365 and Salesforce often require formal training due to their complexity. For organizations using a custom solution such as Miniloop, onboarding speed may vary depending on how closely the system matches existing workflows and user familiarity. When should a company invest in a custom-built CRM solution? A company should consider a custom-built CRM when their workflows are too specialized for standard solutions, or when per-seat fees make traditional CRMs cost-prohibitive. Custom CRMs become especially attractive for organizations with significant CRM spending, complex data requirements, or the need for infrastructure independence and data ownership. Miniloop is positioned for teams spending $50,000 per year or more on CRM, providing tailored systems to match precise processes. title: MiniMed's Smallest App-Controlled Insulin Pump Now Shipping with the World's Smallest Sensor
summary: MiniMed Flex™ with Instinct, made by Abbott, combines discreet design, up to 15 days of sensor wear and proven automation to reduce the work and interruptions of diabetes management NORTHRIDGE,...
body_text: MiniMed Flex™ with Instinct, made by Abbott, combines discreet design, up to 15 days of sensor wear and proven automation to reduce the work and interruptions of diabetes management NORTHRIDGE, Calif. , Aug. 17, 2026 / PRNewswire / -- MiniMed (Nasdaq: MMED) today announced that the MiniMed Flex™ system is now commercially shipping in the U.S. with the Instinct sensor, made by Abbott. For the first time, people with diabetes can use MiniMed's smallest and only app-controlled insulin pump with the world's smallest sensor, with up to 15 days of wear.1 Diabetes technology has advanced significantly, but it can still place a heavy burden on people who rely on it every day — from thinking about where and how to wear devices to balancing diabetes management with the life they want to live. With Instinct now available with MiniMed Flex™, people have more choice in how they manage their diabetes. The combination of discreet,1* longer-wear technology1 and proven automation is designed to reduce the work and interruptions of diabetes management without sacrificing outcomes. Powered by proven SmartGuard™ technology, MiniMed Flex™ automatically adjusts insulin delivery around the clock, while Meal Detection™ technology† can help compensate when a bolus is occasionally missed or carbohydrates are underestimated. The system holds up to 300 units of insulin and works with the Extended™ infusion set, which can be worn for up to seven days. Real-world data◊ from the MiniMed™ 780G system, which uses the same SmartGuard™ algorithm, has shown users with recommended settings achieve 80% Time in Range,2 including more than 90% overnight.3 "People with diabetes deserve technology that works hard without asking much in return," said Que Dallara, chief executive officer at MiniMed. "That's what we're delivering with MiniMed Flex™. The pump can stay tucked away, the algorithm is working around the clock, and now with Instinct, users can go up to 15 days between sensor changes.1 This is another step toward the hands-free future that MiniMed is building, where diabetes technology does more so people can think about it less." The expanded availability coincides with the launch of a new consumer campaign for MiniMed Flex™, the company's first major marketing campaign since the system's U.S. launch with Simplera Sync™ earlier this summer. Built around the promise, "Nothing comes close to freedom you can feel," the campaign highlights the system's discreet design, app control and 24/7 automation, and how those features can help make diabetes management less intrusive in everyday life. "Diabetes is always with me, but I don't want managing it to be the thing I'm thinking about all day," said Monique La Bomme, who lives with diabetes and uses the MiniMed Flex™ system with the Instinct sensor. "With MiniMed Flex, I can clip it and forget it, use the app when I need to interact with it, and go longer between sensor changes. It all adds up to spending less time thinking about my diabetes and more time enjoying life." The MiniMed Flex™ system is FDA cleared for people with type 1 diabetes ages 7 years and older and adults ages 18 years and older with insulin-requiring type 2 diabetes. Customers can order MiniMed Flex™ with Instinct or Simplera Sync™ now. For more information or to get started with MiniMed Flex™, visit www.minimed.com/flex . Frequently Asked Questions What is the MiniMed Flex™ system? The MiniMed Flex™ system is MiniMed's smallest and only app-controlled automated insulin delivery system. Powered by SmartGuard™ technology, it automatically adjusts insulin delivery around the clock based on real-time glucose levels and includes Meal Detection™ technology to help compensate when a meal bolus is occasionally missed or carbohydrates are underestimated. What sensors does the MiniMed Flex™ system use? The MiniMed Flex™ system is compatible with MiniMed's latest sensor portfolio, including the Instinct and Simplera Sync™, giving people greater choice in the sensor experience that works best for them. What are the benefits of using MiniMed Flex™ with the Instinct sensor? MiniMed Flex™ with Instinct combines a discreet, app-controlled insulin pump with a small, longer-wear sensor. Instinct provides real-time glucose readings for up to 15 days,1 while SmartGuard™ technology uses glucose data to automatically adjust insulin delivery, helping reduce the work and interruptions of diabetes management. Who can use the MiniMed Flex™ system? In the U.S., the MiniMed Flex™ system is FDA cleared for people with type 1 diabetes ages 7 and older and adults ages 18 and older with insulin-requiring type 2 diabetes. About MiniMed MiniMed is a global leader in insulin delivery, constantly advancing therapies that support people with diabetes in 80 countries. Our full-stack, integrated ecosystem, including our insulin delivery systems, CGMs, algorithms, and easy-to-use app experience, is designed to work seamlessly together, supported by white-glove, wrap-around service. For over 40 years, we've pioneered therapies people can rely on by anticipating needs, reducing burden, and helping make life with diabetes easier. Our mission is to make every day a better day for people with diabetes. title: How to Integrate Digital Payments Into Your Pharmacy
summary: Learn how to add digital payments to your pharmacy workflow and create a convenient checkout experience patients expect—without replacing your PMS.
body_text: A prescription may be ready, but checkout can still create extra work. Patients may need to ask about a copay at the counter, enter a card, sign for an order, and wait in line, often while your team is managing phones, pickups, and clinical questions. There is also a revenue reality behind every ready prescription: dispensing an order does not guarantee the patient will come in promptly to pay. When payment depends on an in-person visit, outstanding balances can create more follow-up for your team and delay revenue your pharmacy has already earned. ‍ Integrating digital payments for pharmacies means connecting a secure way to pay with the rest of the prescription workflow, from ready notification through pickup or delivery, so patients and staff have a clear, simple next step. ‍ Why isn’t payment processing the whole patient experience? ‍ Your pharmacy management system (PMS) remains the operational system of record and is built to support dispensing and the core workflows that keep your pharmacy moving. ‍ Payment functionality is one important touchpoint, but a connected patient journey includes more: a clear notification, relevant prescription context, payment, applicable signature or approval steps, pickup or delivery updates, and an easy way to ask a question when needed. ‍ Patients are accustomed to modern retail experiences where they can see an order, select fulfillment, pay from their phone, and receive confirmation. They increasingly expect that same clarity from their pharmacy without losing access to the pharmacist they know and trust. ‍ The opportunity is not to replace your PMS. Instead, it’s to make the patient-facing experience around it easier, so your staff can spend less time coordinating disconnected steps and more time delivering the personal care that sets an independent pharmacy apart. ‍ What does a connected digital checkout workflow look like? ‍ A strong pharmacy digital payment solution connects the steps patients and staff already take every day: Your team processes the prescription in its existing PMS. When the order reaches the appropriate status, the patient receives a secure notification. The patient reviews relevant order details, completes pharmacy mobile checkout, and takes any eligible approval or signature actions. Staff can see the order and payment status, then prepare pickup or delivery. The pharmacy retains a clear record for reconciliation and follow-up. ‍ This creates fewer disconnected handoffs between “Rx ready,” “patient contacted,” “payment taken,” and “order completed.” It can also help your pharmacy capture revenue sooner by giving patients a convenient way to pay when they are notified. Patients gain a more confident path forward: they know what is ready, what they owe, and what to do next. ‍ Digital checkout should support, not replace, required counseling, identity verification, controlled-substance procedures, or your pharmacy’s own policies. The goal is to streamline appropriate administrative steps while preserving the clinical and compliance processes your team relies on. ‍ What should you look for when integrating digital payments? ‍ When evaluating pharmacy payment integration, start with the workflow, not just the transaction. The right solution should help your team create a consistent experience from prescription ready to fulfillment. ‍ Look for a platform that: Works with your PMS and the workflow states your pharmacy already uses Gives patients a clear mobile experience, not simply a standalone payment request Connects payment with order status, pickup or delivery, receipts, and applicable signatures Gives staff visibility into paid, pending, and exception orders Supports refunds, reporting, reconciliation, and audit readiness Includes rollout support and patient communications not just technical setup ‍ This checklist helps distinguish “we have a way to accept payment” from “we have a connected digital checkout experience.” The difference matters because every unclear handoff can create more patient questions, staff follow-up, counter congestion, or a prescription that is ready but still unpaid. A connected experience helps make payment a timely, visible part of fulfillment instead of a separate task your team must chase. ‍ How does NimbleRx help pharmacies deliver a more modern experience? ‍ This is where a pharmacy-specific patient engagement and checkout layer can add value alongside your PMS. ‍ NimbleRx does not ask pharmacies to abandon the PMS that runs their day-to-day operations. It integrates with supported pharmacy workflows and adds a patient-facing experience that can be difficult to deliver through a transaction alone. ‍ With NimbleRx, a prescription-ready notification can guide patients through one connected experience to manage the next step: review their order, pay digitally, complete relevant signature or approval actions, and prepare for pickup or delivery. This creates modern retail-like convenience with pharmacy-specific workflows. ‍ Convenience is not simply accepting a card online. It is reducing uncertainty for patients, reducing manual follow-up for staff, and helping pharmacies collect payment sooner on prescriptions that are ready to be fulfilled. NimbleRx also brings related engagement tools, including refill reminders and two-way messaging, into the same patient journey. That helps independent pharmacies give patients the mobile-first clarity they expect while keeping the local pharmacy relationship at the center. ‍ Where should you start? ‍ Map the current route from “Rx ready” to “picked up”, including when and how payment is collected. Identify where patients or staff get stuck: Is it the initial notification, the payment step, a signature, a delivery decision, a status question, or the follow-up required when an order is ready but unpaid? ‍ Then evaluate technology that improves that moment without introducing another manual system. A connected checkout experience can make each next step clearer for patients and more manageable for your team. ‍ Talk to our team to see how NimbleRx connects digital checkout, patient communications, and fulfillment with your existing pharmacy workflow. ‍

title: Alliance Entertainment Reports Strong Engagement at Record Store Day Summer Camp
summary: Alliance Entertainment’s sales organization and AMPED Distribution division met with hundreds of independent retailers and more than 15 supported labels during the July 27-30 event in New Orleans SUNRISE, Fla., Aug. 10, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) — Alliance Entertainment (Nasdaq: AENT), together with its distribution arm, AMPED Distribution, maintained a significant presence at this year’s Record...
body_text: SUNRISE, Fla., Aug. 10, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) — Alliance Entertainment (Nasdaq: AENT), together with its distribution arm, AMPED Distribution, maintained a significant presence at this year’s Record Store Day Summer Camp, held in New Orleans from July 27 through July 30. During the four-day event, Company representatives met with hundreds of independent retail accounts to review current business performance, align on upcoming releases and product initiatives, and plan jointly for the coming selling season. Alliance Entertainment showcased the continued growth of its collectibles business, including its Handmade by Robots brand, alongside other product categories demonstrating strong momentum at independent retail. These meetings were supported by numerous Alliance Entertainment sales representatives and executives, affording retail partners direct access to the personnel responsible for their accounts. AMPED Distribution hosted a dedicated meeting space at the event, which was attended by more than 15 supported labels alongside independent retailers. Representatives from the independent retail community met with many of these labels to review upcoming releases and to discuss the continued growth and support of their business as the company’s independent segment expands. In addition to the scheduled meetings, discussions throughout the event centered on several recurring themes: the continued growth of Record Store Day, the sustained expansion of the vinyl record category, and the resurgence of the compact disc, a subject raised in nearly every conversation with customers. Record Store Day continues to advance the interests of independent retail stores through events of this nature, a format that has proven particularly valuable for engaging a substantial number of key customers in a single venue. “We are very pleased with the results of this year’s Record Store Day Summer Camp event,” said Ken Glaser, Senior Vice President of Sales at Alliance Entertainment. “It is not often where we can meet with so many of our key customers in one place. In addition to our customers, many of our music vendors were there to support the event as well. We look forward to continuing our support for this great event.” About Alliance Entertainment Alliance Entertainment (NASDAQ: AENT) is a premier distributor and fulfillment partner for the entertainment and pop culture collectibles industry. With more than 340,000 unique in-stock SKUs – including over 57,300 exclusive titles across compact discs, vinyl LPs, DVDs, Blu-rays, and video games – Alliance offers the largest selection of physical media in the market. Our vast catalog also includes licensed merchandise, toys, retro gaming products, and collectibles, serving over 35,000 retail locations and powering e-commerce fulfillment for leading retailers. Alliance also owns and operates proprietary collectibles brands, including Handmade by Robots™, a stylized vinyl figure line featuring licensed characters from leading entertainment franchises, and Alliance Authentic™, a premium platform for authentic, certified, and individually numbered entertainment collectibles. In addition, Alliance operates Endstate Authentic, a dedicated NFC-enabled authentication and digital product identity platform supporting authenticated collectibles, resale, and brand protection. Leveraging decades of operational expertise, exclusive sourcing relationships, and a capital-light, scalable infrastructure, Alliance connects fans and collectors to the products, franchises, and experiences they value across formats and generations. title: How Cross-Functional Teams Deliver Exceptional Results
summary: Learn to lead high-performing cross-functional teams that rely on clear priorities and accountability.
body_text: How Cross-Functional Teams Deliver Exceptional Results Published: 8/7/2026 Table of Contents What Are Cross-Functional Teams? Why Cross-Functional Teams Succeed or Struggle How to Structure a Cross-Functional Team: 3 Factors to Consider How Leaders Drive Accountability in Cross-Functional Teams Communication and Role Clarity in Cross-Functional Teams Cross-Functional Teams as a Vehicle for Organizational Change Build Cross-Functional Teams That Turn Priorities Into Results When cross-functional teams work well, they are one of the most powerful structures an organization can build. Their unique composition allows the team to draw expertise from across the business, break through the silos that slow decisions, and align collective capability behind priorities that require more than any one department can deliver. The organizations that build them well tend to solve harder problems and execute more consistently through the kind of conditions that would stall a more fragmented approach. However, most cross-functional teams encounter friction at the execution layer, where shared goals compete with departmental priorities and accountability is harder to maintain without shared reporting lines. Below, we’ll examine what strong cross-functional teams look like in practice and how leaders can empower them to drive exceptional results. Key Takeaways: A cross-functional team is a group of individuals from different departments, disciplines, or areas of expertise who work together toward a shared objective. Cross-functional teams are most effective when shared priorities are clearly defined and protected from competing departmental demands. The most common failure mode in cross-functional collaboration is unclear accountability for shared outcomes, even when communication appears adequate. Leaders of cross-functional teams create the conditions for execution by establishing clear goals, defined roles, and a consistent rhythm of follow-through. What Are Cross-Functional Teams? A cross-functional team is a group of people, usually from different departments, that work together toward a goal that no single function could achieve on its own. Cross-functional teams differ from traditional project teams in that members retain their functional expertise while contributing to a shared objective, rather than setting aside their discipline to work generically. Organizations often deploy cross-functional teams for product launches, process improvement initiatives, and customer experience programs. Each of these contexts requires coordinated input from roles that would otherwise operate independently, making cross-functional collaboration essential to delivering shared results. In a modern environment where speed and adaptability matter more than ever, the ability to draw expertise from across the organization and direct it toward a single goal is a meaningful competitive advantage. Cross-Functional Teams vs. Traditional Teams Traditional teams operate within a single function and report through a single management structure. Conversely, cross-functional teams draw members across that structure, creating both the breadth of perspective that drives innovation and the complex accountability challenges that require careful leadership. This structural difference also shapes how authority functions. In a traditional team, reporting lines naturally clarify ownership. In a cross-functional team, ownership requires explicit definition from the outset. Members often carry dual loyalties to both their home department and to the shared goal. Leaders who develop the capacity to navigate that tension build more durable accountability structures from the start. Why Cross-Functional Teams Succeed or Struggle FranklinCovey research reveals that 92% of employees spend multiple hours each week waiting for clarity or resolving misalignment. Cross-functional collaboration addresses a core source of that friction. Organizations with effective cross-functional teams reduce the handoff delays between departments that slow decisions and obscure risk until it becomes expensive to address. Beyond reducing friction, cross-functional teams also accelerate organizational learning. Members carry knowledge back to their home departments, improving how those functions operate independently, even after the shared project concludes. That spillover effect means the organizational value of an effective cross-functional team extends well beyond its immediate deliverables. Over time, organizations that use cross-functional teams consistently build “connective tissue” between departments that make future collaboration faster and less costly to coordinate. Still, cross-functional teams aren’t without their drawbacks. These teams may underperform when the shared goal is too broad, too distant, or too disconnected from how individual members are measured in their home functions. Execution discipline begins with naming a goal specific enough that the team can track progress week over week. Without that specificity, effort diffuses and accountability becomes difficult to enforce across functions. Download our workbook, 4 Steps to Refine and Execute Your Team Goals , to align your cross-functional team around the results that matter most. How to Structure a Cross-Functional Team: 3 Factors to Consider Building a strong cross-functional team begins with the right mix of people. When building a cross-functional team, organizations should consider three factors: Expertise. Team members should bring the expertise that the work demands, allowing them to contribute the capabilities that are essential to achieving the team’s objective and reflect the perspective of their functional discipline. Decision-making authority. Members who cannot make decisions or commit resources on behalf of their function create bottlenecks that slow progress and increase dependencies. Cross-functional team members need to be empowered to make autonomous decisions in their area of responsibility. Dedicated capacity. Individuals stretched across too many competing priorities often contribute inconsistently, making coordination and accountability more difficult. Team members should have adequate capacity to contribute regularly, rather than participating in name only. Clear roles established early help prevent friction later. Defining who owns decisions, who is accountable for outcomes, and who should be consulted or informed creates a common understanding of responsibilities before conflicts and competing priorities emerge. How Leaders Drive Accountability in Cross-Functional Teams When your team begins to see a big goal moving as a direct result of their efforts, they will know they are winning. And we have found nothing that drives the morale and engagement of a team more than winning. — Chris McChesney, co-author of The 4 Disciplines of Execution Unlike traditional team structures, cross-functional team leaders rarely manage through direct authority. Instead, their influence depends on the clarity they provide, the trust they build, and the team’s conviction that the shared goal is worth the coordination cost it requires. That influence is most effective when it focuses on maintaining clear goals and consistently holding team members to the commitments they’ve made to each other. Leaders who grant decision-making autonomy to cross-functional teams move faster and build stronger ownership. In contrast, teams that are required to escalate routine decisions to a single leader become dependent and slow, undermining the structural advantage cross-functional teams are designed to provide. Building accountability in this context requires leaders to create the conditions for ownership rather than enforcing it through hierarchy. Building a Cadence of Accountability Across Functions Leaders strengthen accountability in cross-functional teams through clear commitments, visible measures of progress, and consistent follow-through. Establishing a cadence of accountability , where team members regularly review commitments and discuss results, reinforces execution discipline and creates a predictable rhythm for collaboration. Visible measures of progress and celebrating wins will keep the team’s objective at the center of its work and make ownership explicit. When team members can quickly see where momentum is strong and where work has stalled, conversations become more focused on removing obstacles and maintaining forward progress rather than simply reporting status. Trust Strengthens Shared Accountability Cross-functional accountability depends heavily on trust . Because team members don’t typically share reporting lines, they need to possess confidence in one another’s follow-through to sustain the commitments that connect their daily work. FranklinCovey research shows that only 42% of employees view their own leader as trusted. That gap makes the candid conversations and mutual accountability that cross-functional teams rely on more difficult to maintain. Leaders strengthen trust by clarifying expectations and creating an environment where challenges can be surfaced without blame. High-trust environments support stronger collaboration across functions. Team members are more willing to ask for help, acknowledge delays, and address issues before they grow into larger conflicts. Over time, that openness helps teams maintain alignment and sustain execution against shared goals. Learn how high-trust leaders and teams achieve outstanding results when you download our guide, Trust & Inspire™: The Leadership Framework Built for Disruption . Communication and Role Clarity in Cross-Functional Teams In most organizations, only 15% of the front line can name the most important goals of the team. The further from the top of the organization they are, the lower the clarity. — Sean Covey, co-author of The 4 Disciplines of Execution Communication in cross-functional teams carries higher stakes than in traditional single-function teams because members interpret information through different functional lenses. What is obvious to one discipline is often opaque to another, and assumptions left unaddressed produce misalignment that compounds across the life of a project. Leaders need strong communication strategies that account for these differences to enable effective cross-functional work. When cross-functional teams align purpose with performance , communication becomes more disciplined and shared goals stay visible even when day-to-day pressures compete for attention. Leaders need to establish clear communication norms early to give their teams a strong foundation, including: Shared understanding of how decisions are made and documented across functions, so ownership is clear and doesn’t need to be renegotiated after the fact. Regular check-ins structured around progress against shared goals rather than departmental updates, keeping the team focused on what it collectively owns. Consistent processes for surfacing assumptions and flagging concerns early, before misalignment has time to compound across functions. Role clarity and communication norms reinforce each other. When each member knows what they own and how decisions are made, communication and collaboration become more precise and friction slows considerably. This clarity also reduces the time teams spend renegotiating ownership when priorities shift, freeing up energy for the work itself. Organizations that establish these norms early in the team’s lifecycle tend to sustain execution quality better than those that address them after misalignment has already taken hold. Reinforce clarity and collaboration when you download our guide, From Misunderstood to Magnetic: A Leader’s Guide to Clear Communication . Cross-Functional Teams as a Vehicle for Organizational Change Cross-functional teams are often the mechanism through which organizations execute strategic change. When a shift in direction requires capability from multiple functions at the same time, a cross-functional team with clear goals and strong accountability structures is more effective than a sequential handoff between departments. Organizational change rarely succeeds when it runs through a single function. Cross-functional teams that operate as execution vehicles develop the ability to align expertise from across the organization and put resources behind the priorities that matter most. Keeping Cross-Functional Teams Focused Through Change When organizational priorities shift, cross-functional teams are among the first to feel pressure from competing demands. Leaders who maintain a visible scoreboard of shared commitments and actively protect the team’s focus during periods of change sustain execution discipline exactly when it is most at risk. Executing strategy through a cross-functional team requires leaders who can hold the line on shared goals while managing the external pressures that seek to redirect the team’s attention. Organizations that develop this leadership capacity are better positioned to lead teams through change without losing the focus that drives results. Download our guide, The Energy of Change , to reveal five essential leadership behaviors that drive collective action in a fluid landscape. Build Cross-Functional Teams That Turn Priorities Into Results Organizations that see the best results from cross-functional teams treat role clarity and accountability as prerequisites rather than afterthoughts. Clear expectations and consistent follow-through separate high-performing teams from merely well-intentioned ones. Ultimately, success depends on whether leadership practices and operating systems give teams what they need to deliver on the priorities that matter most. Organizations that build those systems deliberately are far more likely to achieve the results that cross-functional teams were designed to produce. Those systems are only as effective as the leaders responsible for putting them into practice. As work becomes more interconnected, the ability to lead across functions has become a critical organizational capability. Organizations increasingly rely on leaders who can align teams and maintain accountability across organizational boundaries. Developing those capabilities is essential to improving execution and sustaining long-term performance. Learn how great leaders build high-performing teams and create breakthrough results in today’s evolving landscape.

title: Tracking profits: The Road to Financial Stability
body_text: Hello, passionate trucking owners and life-long learners. I’d like to introduce a 10-article series that will dig into the most common mistakes we see owner-operators make. We’ve worked with hundreds of owner-operators over the years at TrueNorth. We’ve cataloged the most common habits of successful carriers -- as well as the most common pitfalls of those who did not succeed -- to create this list. The first thing I see expert carrier owners do as they prepare for their year ahead is to set targets for overall revenue, costs, and profit. This sounds simple, but there are a lot of factors that go into calculating your profit per mile and over time. I remember doing this with my cousin Tom as he prepared to start his own business. I’ve been lucky to watch him evolve his method over time, and to witness other carriers use these metrics as their north stars to guide them to profits year after year. We’ve made a Profit Calculator app to make this method easily available to everyone, pre-loaded with values for a standard Dry Van truck. You’ll be able to run different scenarios and see how the results compare -- a feature we weren’t able to find in existing online calculators. Read on below to see the factors that go into the calculations. How to calculate your profit per mile and over time Map out your Fixed and Variable Costs Fixed costs are costs you’ll incur even if you stay put. For example, even if you don’t haul freight in a given week, you’ll still need to make your truck payment. Variable costs are costs you only incur when you drive. The largest of these is fuel -- fuel can account for 50% of your total expenses when prices are high, like they are now! Set revenue, mileage, and time off targets The two factors that will most affect your end-of-year profits are Weekly Revenue and Weekly Mileage. It’s important to show these two numbers accurately, otherwise your end result will not reflect reality. We also account for time off, as those are weeks you’ll be incurring Fixed Costs with no revenue. Run the math If you’re using our Profit Calculator , you just click “Save” and you’ll see the results in the History tab. If you’d like us to walk you through the step-by-step calculations, please email support@truenorth.com and we’d be happy to set up a session with you. The most common mistake that kills profits The #1 failure mode we see is not accounting for Opportunity Cost . The Profit Calculator lays that mistake bare when you think about Fixed Costs vs Variable Costs. For example, imagine you’ve landed in the Denver area and rates are $1.50 to get out of the region. Your calculated Cost Per Mile (CPM) is $1.55, so you know you’ll lose money if you take a load at $1.50. In most cases, it would be a mistake to sit until rates increase . You may not get a good-paying load for many days. If you were to sit for 48 hours, you’d incur about $400 in fixed costs and you’d lose out on $1600 of potential revenue. Your opportunity cost is $2000, not $400. You would have been better off taking that $1.50 load into a hot market zone , like Chicago. You’d have earned $1300 and still have had time on your clock to pick up your next load, which earned a healthy $2.90 per mile. Tell us what you think I’d love to hear how you put our Profit Calculator to use, and if you have any suggestions on how to improve it. Please email marketing@truenorth.com and mention the calculator, and I’ll personally review every response. Happy hauling, Jin Stedge TrueNorth CEO
