title: BESS and UPS roles in large data center power architectures
summary: Learn how UPS and BTM BESS architectures differ, how they work together, and how each supports resilience, flexibility, and AI power smoothing.
body_text: Learn how UPS and BTM BESS architectures differ, how they work together, and how each supports resilience, flexibility, and AI power smoothing. Download the white paper As large data centers exceed 50 MW and become more tightly coupled to grid constraints, energy storage is becoming a more important design consideration. Two technologies are often discussed together: double-conversion online uninterruptible power supply (UPS) systems and behind-the-meter battery energy storage systems (BESS). Both use batteries and power conversion, but they serve different roles. A UPS protects critical loads with conditioned, no-break power, while a conventional behind-the-meter (BTM) BESS supports site-level energy management, flexibility, and longer-duration reserve energy. This white paper explains the architectural differences between standard UPS and BESS implementations, where their roles overlap, and how they work together to support resilience, grid responsiveness, and AI power smoothing. Inside, data center operators can understand: The key architectural difference: How series vs. parallel connection shapes power flow, response, and protection capability. Where each technology fits: UPS for critical-load protection and power conditioning; BESS for site-level energy management, peak shaving, and grid services. How AI workloads change the equation: Why synchronized graphics processing unit (GPU) cluster power swings require coordinated mitigation across multiple power-system levels. Practical next steps: Guidance for interconnection planning, simulation, and integrated architecture design. Why this matters now Grid constraints, interconnection requirements, and AI-driven load variability are changing how large data center power systems are planned. Operators that understand where UPS and BESS responsibilities differ and how the two can work together will be better positioned to improve resilience, manage energy more flexibly, and support increasingly dynamic AI workloads. Download the white paper now to get the clarity to make smarter power architecture decisions for the AI era.

title: How to Learn Spanish in a Week: A Realistic Beginner's Plan
summary: A week before a trip to Mexico, most beginners want one thing: the ability to hold a real conversation without freezing mid-sentence. A focused, realistic plan…
body_text: A week before a trip to Mexico, most beginners want one thing: the ability to hold a real conversation without freezing mid-sentence. A focused, realistic plan can genuinely move the needle in seven days, but it requires knowing what to prioritize and what to skip entirely. The best way to learn conversational Spanish fast is to practice the way people actually speak, through repetition, listening, and speaking out loud rather than memorizing grammar rules in isolation. Parrot is built around exactly that approach, putting learners inside real conversations so words connect to meaning quickly. For anyone starting from zero, learn spanish with a tool that mirrors natural speech patterns makes every session count. Table of Contents Can You Really Learn Spanish in a Week? What Research Says About Learning Spanish in One Week Why Most One-Week Spanish Plans Fall Short A Practical 7-Day Spanish Learning Plan Is One Week the Right Goal for You? How Parrot Helps You Make the Most of Your First Week Start Learning Spanish Today Summary Reaching conversational fluency in Spanish takes English speakers roughly 600 to 750 hours of study, according to the Foreign Service Institute. That number reframes what a single week is actually for. Seven days is not a finish line. It is a starting point, and the quality of that start determines how quickly the following weeks compound. The brain consolidates new language during rest and sleep, not just during active study. This means short, repeated sessions distributed throughout the day produce stronger retention than a single long block of cramming. A week of structured daily exposure, even 60 to 90 minutes spread across listening, speaking, and review, builds neural patterns that a six-hour study marathon cannot replicate. Most short-term Spanish plans fail because learners try to cover too much surface area instead of going deep on what matters. Switching between apps, saving podcasts, and memorizing long vocabulary lists creates the feeling of productivity without the repetition that retention actually requires. Words learned through repeated meaningful exposure in context outlast words memorized from lists by a significant margin. Speaking is not the reward at the end of preparation. It is part of the preparation itself. Learners who delay speaking until they feel ready rarely reach that threshold on their own, because passive study does not build the muscle memory that producing language requires. Even basic shadowing, repeating short audio clips after native speakers, or describing nearby objects in simple sentences, builds communication instincts that reading and reviewing never touch. A returning learner who studied Spanish years ago will recover vocabulary and listening instincts far faster than a true beginner. The neural pathways already exist and simply need reactivation. That distinction matters when setting realistic expectations for a one-week plan, because recognition is faster than acquisition, and the two experiences feel very different in practice. Written goals produce measurably better outcomes than vague intentions. According to Mooncamp's goal-setting research, people who write down their goals are 42% more likely to achieve them. A specific target, such as understanding a slow-paced conversation about food or travel and responding with basic sentences, gives a week of focused input something concrete to reach, rather than the immeasurable standard of "learning Spanish." Parrot's Learn Spanish addresses this directly by using short-form video immersion to deliver comprehensible input inside the idle minutes already scattered through a learner's day, connecting words to real conversational meaning rather than drilling them in isolation. Can You Really Learn Spanish in a Week? You can make real progress in Spanish within a week . You will not become fluent. Those are two different things , and mixing them up is where most learners go wrong before they even begin. "The gap between making progress and achieving fluency is where learner expectations collapse: where smart study strategies begin to matter most." ⚠️ Warning: Confusing real progress with full fluency is the single most common mistake new Spanish learners make. It kills motivation before the journey starts. The difference matters because your expectations shape your method . If you spend seven days trying to absorb grammar conjugations and vocabulary lists , you will likely feel defeated by day three . But if you spend those same seven days building the habit of listening to Spanish, absorbing high-frequency phrases in context, and training your ear to recognize natural speech patterns , you walk away with something genuinely useful — not a certificate, but a foundation . 💡 Tip: Focus your first week on high-frequency phrases and active listening — not grammar drills. This approach builds a real, usable foundation far faster than traditional methods. Approach Result After 7 Days Grammar conjugations + vocabulary lists Likely frustrated and overwhelmed by day three High-frequency phrases + active listening Genuine foundation with recognizable speech patterns 🎯 Key Point: The goal of week one is not fluency — it's building a sustainable habit and a functional ear for the language. Why does your method matter more than your motivation? The problem usually isn't the person learning—it's the method being used. Most people study Spanish the way they studied for school tests: cramming information, repeating it, testing themselves, and feeling discouraged when they forget. That cycle creates stress, not real learning. According to Expanish , English speakers need about 600 to 750 hours of study to reach professional working proficiency in Spanish. However, the research shows something equally important: the hours accumulate. Every study session conducted correctly builds on the previous one. Why do phrase books and word lists fail to stick? The common approach to short-term language learning relies on phrase books and translation apps. People memorize "100 Spanish words to know before your trip" and struggle when native speakers respond at natural speed. Isolated words without context are nearly impossible to retain. Your brain stores language as patterns, associations, and meaning tied to sound, not as a list. When you learn "gracias" by hearing it said warmly after a favor, it lands differently than reading it off a flashcard. Tools like Parrot use short-form video immersion to connect words to real conversational moments rather than drilling them in isolation, so five minutes of practice becomes meaningful input instead of rote repetition. What can you realistically achieve in seven days? What you can realistically achieve in seven days is more specific than most guides admit. You can build a working vocabulary of 150 to 200 high-frequency words and phrases, train your ear to catch the rhythm of spoken Spanish, and learn to introduce yourself, ask basic questions, and respond to simple prompts without freezing. According to Expanish , most English speakers reach conversational fluency in six to nine months of consistent practice. A week is not the finish line—it is the starting line, and how you run it determines how quickly the rest of the race goes. The most honest thing anyone can tell you about learning Spanish in a week is this: the goal is not to arrive somewhere by Sunday. The goal is to build the right habit on Monday so that the weeks that follow move you forward. What Research Says About Learning Spanish in One Week Progress in Spanish is measured by hours of quality exposure , not calendar days. According to the Foreign Service Institute via Parrot Blog , reaching upper-intermediate Spanish proficiency requires 600 to 750 hours of study. A single week is a deposit toward that goal , not a complete withdrawal. "Reaching upper-intermediate Spanish proficiency requires 600 to 750 hours of study — a single week is a deposit , not a complete withdrawal." — Foreign Service Institute via Parrot Blog Spanish proficiency develops progressively, with each milestone requiring significantly more practice: Basic survival phrases — ~30–50 hours – Enough to handle greetings, numbers, simple requests, and other essential interactions. Conversational beginner — ~150–200 hours – Supports simple back-and-forth conversations on familiar topics. Upper-intermediate fluency — ~600–750 hours – Enables more complex conversations along with stronger reading and writing ability. 🔑 Takeaway: One week of study cannot deliver fluency — but it can deliver meaningful, measurable progress if your hours are high-quality and focused . 💡 Tip: Instead of asking "Can I learn Spanish in a week?" ask "How many quality hours can I log this week?" — that reframe is the real key to accelerating your long-term progress . ⚠️ Warning: Treating a 7-day sprint as a complete learning solution sets you up for disappointment. Think of it as unlocking the first layer of a 600+ hour journey . How does your brain actually build Spanish in seven days? When you start learning Spanish, your brain builds a network of sound patterns, associations, and meaning—not storing vocabulary like files in a folder. Cognitive science research shows the brain consolidates new language during sleep and rest, not just during active study. A week of short, repeated sessions scattered throughout each day produces stronger retention than one exhausting six-hour block. The spacing effect determines whether learners remember what they studied. Why do most learning habits collapse before the week is up? Most learners use apps that reward streaks and punish gaps, opening gamified lessons and tapping through vocabulary cards. But when the streak breaks or novelty fades, the habit collapses because it was built on obligation, not absorption. Apps like Parrot take a different path, using short-form video immersion to transform idle minutes—a commute, a coffee break, a few moments before bed—into genuine Spanish exposure rather than another task to complete. How much can realistically change in a week? According to Expanish , most English speakers need six to nine months to reach conversational fluency. One week cannot teach you to discuss your childhood or debate politics in Spanish. It can help your brain adjust to the language's sounds, teach you common words and phrases, and help you recognize patterns in real speech rather than translate word by word. This shift from decoding to recognizing marks the first real milestone in language learning, and a focused week can get you there. What kind of study habits make the biggest difference in week one? The learners who get the most from a single week study in a way their brain can use: through comprehensible input, spaced repetition , and consistent daily exposure rather than desperate sprints toward fluency. Build that habit in week one, and every week that follows builds on it. Effort goes into vocabulary lists that don't stick , grammar tables that don't transfer , and apps that reward streaks over understanding . "The brain doesn't retain language through passive exposure — it requires active, meaningful engagement to move words from short-term to long-term memory ." — Language Acquisition Research ⚠️ Warning: If your Spanish plan relies on rote memorization or streak-based apps , you're building on a foundation that won't hold when it matters most. 💡 Tip: The most effective language learners focus on contextual usage and active recall — not just logging daily app minutes or copying grammar tables by hand. Common language-learning methods can build useful foundations, but they may fall short when the goal is practical communication: Vocabulary lists – Words learned without context can be harder to retain and use naturally. Grammar tables – Memorising rules does not necessarily translate into fluent, spontaneous speech. Streak-based apps – Rewards can encourage consistency, but completing daily activities does not always mean the learner has developed genuine understanding. The coverage trap The most common pattern is learning too much surface area instead of going deep on what matters. A learner spends day one memorizing 200 nouns, day two studying verb conjugations, and day three switching to a new app with a different approach entirely. By day five, nothing has been consolidated because nothing was encountered often enough, in context, to register. Research on vocabulary acquisition consistently shows that words retained through repeated meaningful exposure outlast words memorized from lists by a significant margin. Breadth feels productive. Depth is. Why does grammar study slow conversational progress down? Grammar deserves a specific mention because it consumes time that listening should own. Reading about the subjunctive is not the same as recognizing it when a native speaker uses it at natural speed. Grammar knowledge can support comprehension, but it cannot replace it. When your goal is conversational Spanish within a week, grammar is a reference tool, not a curriculum. What happens when you wait until you feel ready to speak? Most learners delay speaking until they feel ready , and that moment rarely arrives on its own. Speaking is not the reward at the end of preparation; it is part of the preparation itself. Basic activities like repeating phrases aloud, describing nearby objects, or shadowing audio clips build the muscle memory that passive study cannot develop. How does constantly switching resources work against retention? The familiar approach of collecting resources makes all of this worse. Each time you switch resources , it costs you focus time and interrupts the repetition your brain needs to remember things. A short-form video platform like Parrot solves this by delivering understandable language input during idle minutes already scattered through your day, keeping your exposure consistent without requiring a separate study block or new learning context. Perfectionism silences you. When every sentence must be grammatically correct before you speak, you stop speaking. Functional communication—being understood in common situations with imperfect grammar—builds more real-world fluency in a week than flawless written exercises ever will. Not fluency or deep conversations, but a meaningful, achievable outcome . "A focused 7-day plan targeting high-frequency vocabulary and basic sentence patterns gives beginners the critical foothold they need to recognize Spanish as structured language—not random sound." 💡 Tip: Focus your first 7 days on high-frequency words and core sentence patterns —these give you the highest return on your time investment before anything else. 🎯 Key Point: The goal of this plan is not instant fluency—it's a real, measurable foundation : recognizing words, parsing sounds, and building the confidence to keep going. The goal of an effective first week is to build a practical foundation you can continue developing: High-frequency vocabulary – Learn the most common words used in everyday Spanish so you can recognise and understand more of what you hear. Basic sentence patterns – Build simple, functional phrases that you can start using from day one. Listening exposure – Train your ear to recognise Spanish as meaningful language rather than unfamiliar sounds. Working foundation – Create a practical launchpad for progressing toward real conversations beyond the first seven days. Day 1: Start with what you'll actually use Start with words and phrases that appear in almost every conversation: greetings, numbers, common questions , polite expressions, and the present tense of ser, estar, and tener—the three verbs that form the skeleton of everyday Spanish. Spend the last 20 minutes of Day 1 listening to beginner-friendly Spanish audio to train your ear to the language's sound. How you say words matters more than most plans acknowledge. If you learn a word by reading it silently, you'll recognize it when you read it but freeze when you hear it spoken at normal speed. Say every new word aloud and repeat it until it feels natural. Days 2 and 3: Shift from studying to absorbing The critical difference between learners who make progress and those who stall is what they do after Day 1. Most keep studying Spanish; the ones who improve start absorbing it. Watch short beginner videos and listen to simple dialogues. Pay attention to expressions that keep appearing—frequency signals the brain what matters. Why does comprehensible input turn vocabulary into lasting retention? According to the italki Blog , a structured 30-day Spanish plan targets 500 new words in the first seven days. These words become useful only when you encounter them in context, hear them in real sentences, and connect them with meaning rather than memorize them from a list. Comprehensible input converts vocabulary from short-term recall into lasting retention. Days 4 and 5: Use the Spanish you've built A common pattern emerges at this point: learners feel they need more preparation before speaking. They don't. Speaking practice on Day 4 with imperfect grammar produces more progress than waiting until Day 7 with perfect grammar, because producing language forces your brain to retrieve and organize what it has absorbed. What does active speaking practice actually look like on these days? Practice shadowing by repeating short audio clips after native speakers. Describe your surroundings in simple sentences. Role-play ordering food, asking for directions, or checking into a hotel. A 10-minute conversation with a tutor or language exchange partner outweighs an hour of passive review. Why does waiting to speak make the gap harder to close? The familiar approach treats speaking as the final reward after sufficient studying, creating a gap between comprehension and communication that widens over time. Apps like Parrot address this by using short-form video immersion to provide daily exposure to real spoken Spanish in otherwise passive moments. Days 6 and 7: Consolidate, don't expand The failure point in most 7-day plans is Day 6, when learners introduce large amounts of new material instead of strengthening what they already have, resulting in shallow vocabulary with no depth. Spend these final two days revisiting words in their original contexts. Repeat role-play scenarios from Days 4 and 5 and summarise short videos in Spanish using your own words. This active retrieval —pulling language out rather than pushing it in—shifts vocabulary from recognition to use. A daily routine that actually holds The italki Blog notes that you can reach basic conversational ability in Spanish within 30 days with consistent effort. A daily routine looks like this: 20 to 30 minutes of structured lessons covering common vocabulary and core grammar, 20 to 30 minutes of beginner-friendly listening, 10 to 15 minutes of speaking practice through shadowing or simple conversation, and 10 to 15 minutes reviewing words in their natural contexts. That's 60 to 90 minutes a day: manageable, specific, and balanced across every essential skill. Why is the habit itself the real outcome of week one? What most learners miss is that the routine itself is the outcome of week one. The Spanish you learn in seven days will grow, but the habit of daily exposure, listening, speaking, and reviewing in context determines whether your Spanish continues growing six months from now. The goal for a 7-day plan isn't to know Spanish . It's to know how to keep learning it, with a working vocabulary and enough listening exposure that the language feels familiar rather than foreign. Poco a poco. Little by little. That's the only path that works. But whether one week is the right frame for your specific situation deserves consideration before you begin. Is One Week the Right Goal for You? Seven days is the right amount of time — if you know what you're actually measuring. The question isn't whether a week is long enough to learn Spanish — it's whether a week is long enough to build the system that learns Spanish for you . "The goal of the first week isn't fluency — it's building the learning system that makes fluency inevitable ." 🎯 Key Point: One week is not about how much Spanish you can absorb — it's about whether you can establish the habits, tools, and routines that will carry you forward long after day seven. 💡 Tip: Before you start your 7-day sprint , define your success metric clearly. Are you measuring vocabulary words learned , daily consistency , or confidence in basic conversation ? The right goal changes everything about how you structure your week. Effective Spanish learning is less about unrealistic short-term targets and more about building a sustainable system: “Learn Spanish in a week” → Build a daily Spanish habit that compounds over time. Memorize 100+ words randomly → Master core vocabulary systematically through structured repetition and context. Consume as much content as possible → Practise active recall every day to turn exposure into usable knowledge. Finish a course → Create a repeatable routine that continues beyond any single course or programme. What your goal actually determines The honest answer depends on why you're starting. Travel preparation, survival vocabulary, basic greetings and directions can be achieved in a focused week. But if your goal is to have a real conversation with a native speaker at natural speed, one week is the beginning of the timeline, not the end. Treating it as a finish line is where most people go wrong. Does your starting point change how fast you can progress? Where you start changes how the math works. Someone returning to Spanish after a long break can recover vocabulary and listening skills much faster than someone starting from scratch. The neural pathways already exist but lie dormant. A focused week for someone returning to the language can yield progress equivalent to months for a beginner. Why does the most common approach create activity without progress? The most common approach is to download an app and study in daily bursts. This creates activity without necessarily creating progress, since passive familiarity with vocabulary differs from absorbing how the language sounds and flows in real use. Apps like Learn Spanish use short-form video immersion built around comprehensible input, transforming idle minutes into genuine exposure to Spanish as it's spoken, not drilled. How does goal clarity shape what a week of learning can actually achieve? According to Mooncamp's Goal Setting Statistics , people who write down their goals are 42% more likely to achieve them. Writing down what you want constitutes a form of commitment. If your written goal is "speak Spanish confidently," it's too unclear to work toward in seven days. If it's "understand a slow-paced conversation about food or travel and respond with basic sentences," that's a target a week of focused learning can reach. What is the real value of setting a one-week learning goal? The value of a one-week goal isn't the Spanish you build up; it's the learning habit you create or don't. Seven days is long enough to prove that daily practice is doable, fits inside a commute or lunch break, and produces real progress. The learner who continues after week one is the one who eventually has that conversation. body_text: Mobile Infrastructure Reports Second Quarter 2026 Financial Results August 11, 2026 4:05 PM EDT Download as PDF Related Documents Earnings Webcast Audio 10-Q Filing HTML PDF XBRL ZIP Same-Location Revenue Growth in the Second Quarter on Continued Utilization Gains Contract Parking Volumes Grew Approximately 12% Year-over-Year Transient Inflected to Revenue Growth with Reopening of Key Markets Cash Flow Funded Line of Credit Paydown in Second Quarter Conference Call Will be Held on August 11, 2026, at 4:30 PM Eastern Time CINCINNATI, Aug. 11, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Mobile Infrastructure Corporation (Nasdaq: BEEP), (“Mobile”, “Mobile Infrastructure” or the “Company”), the nation’s only publicly traded owner of parking infrastructure, today reported results for the three and six months ended June 30, 2026. “Our second quarter results reflect additional progress against our 2026 plan and initiatives,” noted Stephanie Hogue, Chief Executive Officer. “We are seeing the benefits of our plan to grow revenue by increasing utilization via growth in contract and transient parking, followed by rate. Same-Location Revenue grew 5.6% and Same-Location NOI grew 12.0% year-over-year, showing strong continued momentum throughout the second quarter. Contract parking volumes grew approximately 12.0% year-over-year, benefitting from return-to-office momentum and residential demand. Importantly, transient revenue inflected to growth, increasing 4% year to year. “Transient revenue grew portfolio-wide as several key markets moved toward stabilization following disruptions related to construction and redevelopment projects. This included strength in Cincinnati following the reopening of the Cincinnati Convention Center. Portfolio utilization ended up approximately five percentage points year-over-year on a trailing twelve-month basis. Consistent with our “volume first, rate second” strategy, we prioritized occupancy, and with those gains now established, we are beginning to increase rates across much of the portfolio. We believe this is a clear indication that our strategy is working. “We remained focused on our capital allocation strategy during the second quarter, using $4.5 million to paydown our credit line. We continue to work to sell assets under our 36-month plan for $100 million of asset rotation. To date, we have completed roughly one-third of the program, yielding $33 million of proceeds at a weighted average capitalization rate of about 2%. We believe that these private market values highlight the true value of our assets and the implicit worth of our portfolio, which we believe significantly exceeds the current share price for Mobile Infrastructure shares. We will continue to seek opportunities to strategically rotate assets in an accretive manner.” Second Quarter 2026 Highlights Total revenue was $8.9 million as compared to $9.0 million in the prior-year period and $7.9 million in Q1. Same-Location Revenue was $8.9 million as compared to $8.4 million in the prior-year period and $7.7 million in Q1. Net loss was $3.2 million as compared to $4.7 million in the prior-year period and $7.8 million in Q1. NOI* was $5.8 million as compared to $5.4 million in the prior-year period, an increase of 7.5% year-over-year. Same-Location NOI* was $5.9 million as compared to $5.2 million in the prior-year period, an increase of 12.0% year-over-year, reflecting strong continued momentum. Adjusted EBITDA* was $4.1 million as compared to $3.8 million in the prior-year period, an increase of 5.5% year-over-year. Contract parking volumes grew approximately 12% year-over-year, supported by continued strength in residential and return-to-office momentum. Asset rotation progress remained on track, with cumulative proceeds from non-core asset sales of $33 million toward the Company’s $100 million, three-year strategic asset rotation program. * Explanations of these non-GAAP financial measures and reconciliation to the most comparable GAAP financial measures are presented later in this press release. Q2 2026 Financial Results Total revenue of $8.9 million decreased by 1.1% from $9.0 million in the prior-year quarter, primarily due to the sale of assets in 2025 and 2026. Same-Location Revenue was $8.9 million, an increase of 5.6% compared to $8.4 million in second quarter of 2025. Total property taxes and operating expenses were $3.0 million, as compared to $3.6 million during the second quarter of 2025. General and administrative expenses were $2.6 million, which included $0.8 million of non-cash compensation, compared to $2.4 million during the second quarter of 2025, which included $0.8 million of non-cash compensation. Interest expense was $4.8 million compared to $4.7 million in the second quarter of 2025. Net loss was $3.2 million, an improvement from $4.7 million in the prior-year period. Same-Location Net Operating Income (“Same-Location NOI”), defined by the Company as total revenues less property taxes and operating expenses for the 35 properties owned both reported periods, was $5.9 million, up 12.0% from $5.2 million in the prior-year period, reflecting strong continued momentum across the portfolio. Growth was driven by continued contract and utilization gains – led by the Cincinnati and Cleveland markets – together with active property tax appeal management and disciplined operating expense control. Adjusted EBITDA was $4.1 million compared to $3.8 million in the prior-year period. Revenue Per Available Stall (“RevPAS”) was $224.96, compared to $212.14 in the second quarter of 2025 and $184.23 in the first quarter of 2026. Portfolio utilization was up approximately five percentage points year-over-year on a trailing twelve-month basis, reflecting continued contract growth and the reopening of several demand-driving venues across the portfolio. Balance Sheet, Cash Flow, and Liquidity At June 30, 2026, the Company had $10.9 million in cash, cash equivalents and restricted cash, compared to $15.3 million at December 31, 2025. As of June 30, 2026, total debt outstanding, net, including outstanding borrowings under the Line of Credit and notes payable, was $197.1 million. During the quarter, we paid down $3.7 million of principal and $0.8 million of accrued interest on our Line of Credit. Paydown of the Line of Credit is a primary near-term use of asset sale proceeds. The Company continues to evaluate additional capital allocation opportunities, including share repurchases and asset acquisitions, in coordination with its Board of Directors. Full Year 2026 Guidance** The Company is reiterating its full year 2026 guidance as initially provided with fourth quarter and full year 2025 results. For full year 2026, the Company continues to expect revenue in the range of $35 million to $38 million, representing 4% growth at the midpoint over 2025 results, and 8% growth on a same-location basis. The Company expects NOI to range from $21.5 million to $23.0 million, representing year-over-year growth of 7% at the midpoint, and 10% growth on a same-location basis. The Company expects adjusted EBITDA to range from $15.0 million to $16.5 million, representing year-over-year growth of 10% at the midpoint, and 13% growth on a same-location basis. This guidance is supported by expectations for continued contract volume growth, the reopening and enhancement of several venues, and the positive impact from technology optimization across the Company’s core portfolio on pricing and utilization. The guidance does not reflect any potential future asset sales or acquisitions from the asset rotation plan. **The Company does not provide a reconciliation for non-GAAP estimates on a forward-looking basis, where it is unable to provide a meaningful or accurate calculation or estimation of reconciling items and the information is not available without unreasonable effort. title: Oportun Appoints Scott Scheirman to its Board of Directors

body_text: Oportun Appoints Scott Scheirman to its Board of Directors August 13, 2026 4:20pm EDT Download as PDF SAN MATEO, Calif., Aug. 13, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Oportun (Nasdaq: OPRT), a mission-driven financial services company, today announced Scott Scheirman has joined its Board of Directors as an independent Director, effective August 11, 2026. He will serve as Chair of the Board’s Audit & Risk Committee and as a member of its Compensation & Leadership Committee. With his appointment, Oportun’s Board now includes eight directors. Scheirman brings more than three decades of executive leadership and finance experience across financial services, payments, risk management, and capital markets. He most recently served as President and Chief Executive Officer of CPI Card Group Inc. from October 2017 until his retirement in January 2024, after joining its board of directors in 2016. Previously, Scheirman was Chief Executive Officer and co-founder of JKL Ventures LLC, a private investment and strategic advisory firm. He also served as Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer of The Western Union Company and held executive leadership and financial roles at First Data Corporation, now Fiserv. Scheirman began his career at Ernst & Young LLP and holds a Bachelor of Science degree in Business Administration with an emphasis in Accounting from the University of Northern Colorado. “Oportun is committed to thoughtful Board refreshment and maintaining the right mix of experience and perspectives to support effective oversight. Scott brings significant strategic planning and public company leadership experience as a former CEO and CFO, as well as a deep understanding of financial services, and will be a valuable addition to the Board,” said Ginny Lee, Chair of Oportun’s Nominating, Governance & Social Responsibility Committee. “Scott brings the perspective of an experienced operator and a practical understanding of how strong financial businesses create value over time,” said Doug Bland, Chief Executive Officer of Oportun. “His perspective will be especially valuable as we continue to enhance our strategy, strengthen execution and build sustainable, profitable growth." About Oportun Oportun (Nasdaq: OPRT) is a mission-driven financial services company that puts its members' financial goals within reach. With intelligent borrowing, savings, and budgeting capabilities, Oportun empowers members with the confidence to build a better financial future. Since inception, Oportun has provided more than $22.7 billion in responsible and affordable credit, saved its members more than $2.5 billion in interest and fees, and helped its members set aside an average of more than $1,800 annually. For more information, visit oportun.com . body_text: Zug, 3 August 2026 Decision of the Takeover Board 947/01 dated 30 July 2026 concerning WISeKey International Holding AG / WISeKey International Corp. on the request of WISeKey International Holding AG and WISeKey International Corp. regarding the determination of validity of an opting-out clause On 30 July 2026, the Takeover Board rendered the f­­ollowing decision (unofficial translation of the original German text): It is determined that the opting-out provision in the articles of association of WISeKey International Corp. will be valid and effective under takeover law if this opting-out provision forms part of the articles of association of WISeKey International Corp. no later than the time at which the merger of WISeKey International Holding AG with and into WISeKey International WISeKey International Holding AG shall publish the position statement of its board of directors (if any), the operative part of this decision, and the information regarding the objection right of qualified shareholders in accordance with articles 6 and 7 TOO. This decision will be published on the website of the Takeover Board after WISeKey International Holding AG has made the publication provided for in item 2 of this operative part. The fee payable by WISeKey International Holding AG and WISeKey International Corp., with joint and several liability, amounts to CHF 30,000. Objection (article 58 of the Ordinance of the Takeover Board on Public Takeover Offers; TOO) A shareholder with a holding of at least 3% of the voting rights of WISeKey International Holding SA, whether exercisable or not (a “qualified shareholder”, article 56 TOO), who has not yet participated in the proceedings, may file an objection against the decision of the Takeover Board. The objection must be filed with the Takeover Board within five trading days after the publication of the decision of the Takeover Board. The objection must contain a formal request and a summary of the legal grounds, as well as proof of the holding in accordance with article 56 para. 3 and 4 TOO (article 58 para. 3 TOO). title: A10 Networks Launches A10 AI Gateway, an Intelligent Control Plane for All AI Operations
summary: Turkcell is accelerating the virtualization of its network infrastructure with the support of A10 Networks' advanced software solutions.
body_text: New Offering, Unveiled at Black Hat USA 2026, Brings Integrated Solution for Performance Optimization, Budget Management, Real-time Observability, and Governance Running Entirely within the Customer’s Environment SAN JOSE, Calif., August 13, 2026 – A10 Networks (NYSE: ATEN) today announced the general availability of the A10 AI Gateway , a centralized, intelligent control plane that gives organizations unified routing, cost management, and governance across every AI agent, application and large language model (LLM) they use. The company introduced the A10 AI Gateway last week at Black Hat USA 2026 in Las Vegas, where it was showcased alongside A10’s broader AI portfolio, including the TrojAI by A10 Networks AI security platform. As AI adoption accelerates, developers are increasingly building agents and embedding AI into applications and business systems, drawing on a growing range of models across the enterprise. Without a central control point, teams have little visibility into which models are being used, how they perform, what they cost, and whether workloads are running efficiently. The A10 AI Gateway brings all of those AI interactions into a single, governed environment so organizations can optimize performance, control spend, centralize observability, enforce security, and give developers and users reliable access to the right models. “Enterprises are being asked to move fast on AI and stay in control at the same time. AI use is spreading faster than teams can discover, govern, or secure it, driving up cost and leaving no single place to set the rules. The A10 AI Gateway gives organizations one intelligent control plane to see how AI is being used, to govern who can access which models, and match every request to the right model at the right cost. Our integrated portfolio gives customers a complete, sovereign way to put AI to work at scale. That is how enterprises adopt AI with confidence instead of trading speed for control,” said Dhrupad Trivedi, president and CEO, A10 Networks. Beyond Metering: an Intelligent Control Plane for AI The first generation of AI gateways centralized access, simplified API management, and metered requests across providers. Enterprise AI has since grown far more dynamic, with different teams needing different models, and every request varying in complexity. The A10 AI Gateway goes beyond simply managing AI traffic by intelligently routing each request to the most appropriate model based on the needs of that request, while giving organizations the ability to manage access, usage, and costs at the individual and team levels. Key capabilities of the A10 AI Gateway include: Identity-based AI Access: Organizations apply access and routing policies by individual user and group profile (e.g., engineering vs. finance), in sync with existing local directory systems. Smart Routing: The A10 AI Gateway moves past static routing policies and simple metering. It evaluates the complexity and type of each request and then, with reasoning, routes simple tasks to more cost-efficient models and complex, reasoning-intensive tasks to more capable ones. Centralized Traffic and Cost Management: Acting as a central control plane, the A10 AI Gateway provides real-time, per-request cost tracking in dollars; per-model and per-team token budgets with hard limits and soft-limit alerts; and business-layer rate limiting (TPM/RPM) enforced per key or team, all with centralized visibility into how AI is being used and governed. The result is a more controlled, efficient, and secure approach to enterprise AI, helping organizations maximize the value of every AI interaction while maintaining visibility and control over how AI is accessed and used. Part of A10’s Full-lifecycle Approach to AI The A10 AI Gateway complements A10’s broader AI security portfolio including TrojAI and ThreatX solutions, securing AI across its full lifecycle: tested before deployment, defended at runtime, and enforced at the network and API layer. Delivered as software, or with integrated hardware, that runs entirely within the customer’s own environment, on-premises, in a private cloud, or air-gapped, the portfolio keeps models, data, and policy under the organization’s control with full data sovereignty, an advantage cloud-hosted and edge-bound gateways cannot match. Availability The A10 AI Gateway is available now. summary: All-in-one, AC-coupled system brings Enphase's distributed architecture to commercial, industrial, and multifamily energy storage FREMONT, Calif., Aug. 18, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Enphase Energy, Inc. (NASDAQ: ENPH), a global energy technology company, today opened U.S.
body_text: All-in-one, AC-coupled system brings Enphase's distributed architecture to commercial, industrial, and multifamily energy storage FREMONT, Calif., Aug. 18, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Enphase Energy, Inc. (NASDAQ: ENPH), a global energy technology company, today opened U.S. pre-orders for the IQ® Battery C80, its first commercial battery storage system. The all-in-one, AC-coupled system will deliver 80 kWh of usable energy capacity and up to 40 kVA of continuous power in a single, compact enclosure, with battery packs and microinverters fully integrated. IQ Battery C80 extends Enphase's distributed architecture into commercial energy storage, completing the company's end-to-end commercial offering. It will pair with IQ9N-3P™ and IQ9S-3P™ Commercial Microinverters at 277Y/480 V, as well as IQ8P-3P™ and IQ8H-3P™ Microinverters at 120Y/208 V, enabling complete, all-AC solar-plus-storage systems without central inverters or high-voltage DC coupling. From 80 kWh to 2 MWh, the system is engineered for commercial, industrial, and multifamily applications. Its modular architecture will allow customers to right-size projects and expand storage capacity over time. Its distributed, microinverter-based architecture is designed to reduce single points of failure and support high system uptime. IQ Battery C80 will support demand charge management, time-of-use shifting, solar self-consumption, grid services, and virtual power plant (VPP) participation — helping customers manage energy costs and maximize the value of onsite solar generation. IQ Battery C80 will be available in two three-phase configurations: a 120Y/208 V model delivering 33 kVA for multifamily properties and smaller commercial buildings, and a 277Y/480 V model delivering 40 kVA for larger commercial and industrial applications. Both will use lithium iron phosphate (LFP) chemistry, deliver greater than 90% AC round-trip efficiency, and operate across an ambient temperature range of -22°F to 131°F. Both configurations will support Enphase Power Control software, certified to UL 3141, enabling two-hour or four-hour system designs. Busbar and feeder overload controls will enable flexible wiring, help reduce balance-of-system infrastructure costs, and potentially avoid unnecessary electrical equipment upgrades. The AC-coupled architecture will also allow IQ Battery C80 to pair with third-party commercial three-phase solar inverters for both new and retrofit projects. IQ Battery C80 will use active air cooling without liquid cooling or external HVAC, helping simplify installation and improve reliability. Its integrated battery and power-conversion architecture will also reduce the number of separate components that need to be installed and interconnected. Battery-module-level heating will support reliable operation in cold-weather conditions. IQ Battery C80 is expected to be produced at U.S. manufacturing facilities and to be FEOC compliant. U.S. production can also help certain eligible projects qualify for domestic content bonus tax credits, subject to project-specific requirements and applicable laws. Safety is engineered at the module level. IQ Battery C80 will feature battery-module smoke and gas sensing with active pressure release, along with support for fire alarm control panel integration and emergency stop for safe isolation. The system will be certified to UL 9540A and large-scale fire test protocols for thermal runaway safety and housed in an outdoor-rated NEMA 3R enclosure for pad or floor mounting. “We designed the IQ Battery C80 to make commercial storage simpler to deploy, easier to scale, and more resilient,” said Aaron Gordon, senior vice president and general manager of the systems business unit at Enphase Energy. “With 208 V and 480 V configurations, it will serve applications ranging from multifamily properties to large commercial and industrial facilities.” Pre-orders for the IQ Battery C80 are open now, with shipments expected to begin in the first half of 2027. The system will be backed by a 15-year limited warranty. Customers should consult their legal and tax advisors to confirm eligibility for applicable tax credits and incentives. Learn more about commercial storage on the Enphase website . About Enphase Energy, Inc.
